kurals.tamil:
ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல் அதுவல்லது
ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Eedhal isaipada vaazhdhal adhuvalladhu
Oodhiyam illai uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: To give to those in need, and to live in such a way that praise gathers around one’s name: apart from this, there is no real profit that a living being can earn from life.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a piggy bank you can’t take with you when you leave. The only things you really keep from life are what you gave away and the kind words people say about you because of it. Giving, and being remembered well for it, is the real prize of being alive.
kurals.university: The chapter on Renown opens by fusing it with the preceding chapter on Giving (ஈகை): ஈதல் (giving) and இசைபட வாழ்தல் (living so that isai, praise, arises) are presented as one achievement, gathered by the demonstrative அது (‘that’). The pivotal word is ஊதியம் (wages, income, profit), a commercial term deliberately applied to the உயிர் (the living soul): life is framed as a venture whose only true yield is renown generated by generosity. Classical commentary (Parimelazhagan, echoed by Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah) specifies giving to the poor, which anchors புகழ் in ethical action rather than mere celebrity. The couplet thus redefines ‘gain’: wealth hoarded is not profit; wealth converted into others’ welfare, and the esteem that follows, is. The same link between liberality and lasting worth appears in the Vedic hymn to Liberality and in Aristotle’s remark that the liberal are loved precisely because they give.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn titled ‘Liberality’ says wealth that is shared is never really lost, while the person who refuses to give ends up alone and friendless.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats giving as the one ‘income’ that does not evaporate: the giver’s wealth survives by being given.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on giving as the only lasting gain; the hymn speaks of friendship and comfort rather than fame or praise explicitly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, taking leave of the Ephesian elders, tells them to support the weak and cites Jesus’ saying that giving is more blessed than receiving.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts relocate life’s real gain from what one takes in to what one gives out.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches giving-as-true-gain; lacks the Kural’s emphasis on praise/renown as the fruit of giving.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allāh is like a seed [of grain] which grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pictures charity as a seed that multiplies many hundredfold, so that what is given is not lost but increased.
islam.tie_back: The Kural calls giving the soul’s only profit; the Qur’an likewise frames spending on others as the most fruitful investment a person can make.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on giving-as-multiplied-gain; the reward is divine rather than human praise.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.”
judaism.explanation: Hebrew wisdom literature ranks a good reputation and people’s goodwill above any amount of money.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar says renown is the only real profit; Proverbs says a good name outranks riches. Both place reputation above wealth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on name-over-wealth; Proverbs does not here tie the good name specifically to generosity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts the miser, who gains nothing lasting, with the wise giver, whose generosity alone secures future happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make giving the single act that yields a real, lasting return for a life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on giving as the one true gain; the payoff is happiness hereafter rather than renown in this world.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor elderly couple, alone in their Phrygian village welcome the disguised Jupiter and Mercury and share their meagre food. The gods flood the inhospitable neighbourhood, turn the couple’s cottage into a temple, and at death change them into an oak and a linden that later visitors honour with garlands.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their small act of hospitality is the only thing that distinguishes them, and it becomes the reason they are remembered and honoured ever after.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, humble giving is what converts an ordinary life into an honoured name.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Roman retelling of a Greek-world myth; emphasises divine reward for hospitality more than human praise, but ends in lasting honour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The liberal are almost the most loved of all virtuous characters, since they are useful; and this depends on their giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that generous people win exceptional affection from others, and that this esteem springs directly from their giving.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle and Valluvar both trace a person’s good standing among others back to the act of giving.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on giving leading to esteem; Aristotle does not claim this is life’s only gain.

kurals.tamil:
உரைப்பார் உரைப்பவை எல்லாம் இரப்பார்க்கொன்று
ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uraippaar uraippavai ellaam irappaarkku ondru
Eevaarmel nirkum pukazh.
kurals.meaning: All the praise that speakers and poets utter finally comes to rest on those who give something to people who ask of them.
kurals.elementary: When grown-ups tell stories about great people, the ones everyone loves to talk about are usually the helpers, the ones who shared. Kindness is what people remember and keep talking about.
kurals.university: உரைப்பார் உரைப்பவை, ‘what those who speak speak’, is read by Parimelazhagan as the praise uttered by poets and eulogists; the couplet claims that all of it ultimately ‘stands upon’ (மேல் நிற்கும்) givers. Renown is thus a social fact: it lives in the mouths of others and is conferred, not seized. The verb நிற்கும் (‘stands, abides’) implies durability; the praise settles and remains. Classical Tamil culture institutionalised exactly this in the bardic economy of Sangam patronage, where poets immortalised generous chieftains such as Pari in verse. The couplet therefore doubles as a sociology of reputation: fame follows the flow of gifts, a pattern echoed in the Buddha’s list of the visible fruits of generosity and in the Psalmist’s praise of the one who ‘hath given to the poor’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is for this, O king, that they who have great intelligence say that there is nothing higher and greater in the three worlds than gift!”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Markandeya, instructing Yudhishthira on charity, concludes that the wise unanimously declare giving to be the highest thing in all the worlds.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says all that speakers praise rests on givers; the Mahabharata likewise reports the verdict of the wise converging on the giver.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 199 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on the wise exalting giving; the passage praises the gift itself rather than describing the giver’s social renown.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her.”
christianity.explanation: When a woman pours costly ointment on Jesus and is criticised for waste, he declares that her generous act will be told everywhere in her memory.
christianity.tie_back: A single act of lavish giving becomes what people everywhere speak of, just as the Kural says all praise settles on the giver.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on giving becoming a universally spoken memorial; the gift is devotional rather than to the needy.

islam.quote_or_event: “You people are Allah's witnesses on earth.”
islam.explanation: When a funeral passed and people praised the deceased, the Prophet said Paradise was affirmed for him, explaining that the community’s testimony about a person carries real weight.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat what people say about someone as a meaningful verdict on that life; the Kural adds that such praise gathers around givers.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on public praise as a true measure of a life; the hadith does not specify generosity as the cause of the praise.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness endureth for ever; his horn shall be exalted with honour.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm describes the righteous person who distributes to the poor, promising that his righteousness lasts and his standing is raised in honour.
judaism.tie_back: Giving to the poor leads to enduring honour: nearly the same chain of cause and effect as the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: gift to the poor followed by lasting honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fine reputation of one who gives, who is a master of giving, is spread far & wide.”
buddhism.explanation: Asked by General Siha for a fruit of generosity visible in this life, the Buddha lists, among others, that the generous person’s good reputation travels widely.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the Kural: renown is the visible, spoken-about fruit that settles on the giver.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.34, Siha Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: generosity producing widely spoken reputation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He that is righteous and deals righteously, the people tell of his praise among all lands, and many shall call him blessed.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope, preparing to honour a ragged stranger (the disguised Odysseus), reflects that the harsh are cursed while the righteous are praised everywhere.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts describe praise spreading through people’s speech; Penelope says this while practising generous hospitality.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close on praise spreading across lands; the stated cause is righteousness in general, not giving specifically.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The prize appointed for the noblest deeds; and this is honour; that is surely the greatest of external goods.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle identifies honour as the greatest of the external goods, the recognition that is awarded for the finest actions.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle treats honour as conferred by others for noble deeds, just as the Kural says praise settles on those who give.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on honour as conferred recognition; does not single out giving as its source.

kurals.tamil:
ஒன்றா உலகத்து உயர்ந்த புகழல்லால்
பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன் றில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ondraa ulagaththu uyarndha pukazhallaal
Pondraadhu nirpadhu ondril.
kurals.meaning: In this world, nothing stands without perishing except exalted renown, which has no equal.
kurals.elementary: Toys break, houses get old, and even mountains slowly wear down. But a story about someone who was truly good can be told again and again for a thousand years. Good fame is the one thing that doesn’t wear out.
kurals.university: The syntax hinges on ஒன்றா, which commentators read two ways: as qualifying புகழ் (‘peerless, matchless renown’) or as describing உலகு (‘this world, where nothing stays constant’). Either way, the couplet sets renown against the Indian commonplace of impermanence (நிலையாமை), which Valluvar treats in its own chapter (34): bodies, riches and kingdoms are பொன்றும் (perishable), but உயர்ந்த புகழ், exalted renown, alone stands. This is Valluvar’s this-worldly answer to the question of immortality: not the soul’s survival, but the survival of a good name in human memory. The claim parallels the Greek heroic ideal of kleos aphthiton (‘imperishable fame’), though Valluvar grounds renown in giving rather than martial glory. Philosophers such as the Stoics would dispute it, counting reputation among things outside our control and therefore not a true good.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that fleeing battle would earn him a disgrace that people would talk about forever (the Sanskrit calls the ill-fame avyayā, ‘imperishable’).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita presupposes the Kural’s point from the negative side: reputation, good or bad, outlasts the person and is what endures.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Inverse parallel (enduring infamy rather than enduring renown); the underlying idea that reputation is lasting is shared.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly wealth with imperishable treasure stored with God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts sort things into the perishable and the imperishable, but Jesus locates the imperishable in heaven, Valluvar in renown on earth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the contrast of perishable and lasting goods; differs on what lasts (heavenly treasure, not fame).

islam.quote_or_event: “And grant me a mention [i.e., reputation] of honor among later generations.”
islam.explanation: Abraham prays that he will be remembered with honour by the generations who come after him.
islam.tie_back: A prophet explicitly asks for the very thing the Kural calls the one imperishable possession: an honoured name that outlives him.
islam._accuracy_note: Close: lasting honourable reputation is sought as a real good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says a righteous person’s memory remains a blessing, while the wicked person’s name decays.
judaism.tie_back: Only the good name survives decay: the same contrast between lasting renown and everything that rots away.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on the survival of a righteous name.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even gorgeous royal chariots wear out, and indeed this body too wears out. But the Dhamma of the Good does not age; thus the Good make it known to the good.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that splendid possessions and the body itself decay, but the teaching and way of the good do not grow old.
buddhism.tie_back: Both divide the world into what wears out and the one thing that does not; for Valluvar it is renown, for the Dhammapada the Dhamma of the good.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same structure of perishable versus ageless; the ageless thing is the Dhamma of the good rather than personal fame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Thus even in death your fame, Achilles, has not been lost, and your name lives evermore among all mankind.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld, Agamemnon’s shade tells Achilles that his fame survived his death and lives on among all people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is kleos aphthiton, imperishable fame, the Greek counterpart of Valluvar’s புகழ் that alone does not perish.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on fame as what survives death; Achilles’ fame is martial rather than earned by giving.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus lists reputation among external things that are not truly ours and should not be treated as goods.
philosophy.tie_back: A deliberate counterpoint: where the Kural calls renown the one lasting possession, the Stoic calls it something never really possessed at all.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Honest contrast rather than parallel; included because Stoicism is the major philosophical challenge to valuing renown.

kurals.tamil:
நிலவரை நீள்புகழ் ஆற்றின் புலவரைப்
போற்றாது புத்தேள் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nilavarai neelpukazh aatrin pulavaraip
Potraadhu puththel ulagu.
kurals.meaning: If someone achieves renown that reaches the ends of the earth and endures, the world of the gods will stop honouring even its own celestial sages and honour that person instead.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a class in the sky where the angels usually cheer for their own star students. But if someone down on earth does something so good that the whole world talks about it for ages, even the sky-class stops and cheers for that person instead.
kurals.university: The couplet is deliberately audacious: earthly renown outranks celestial status. Its key term is contested. புலவர் ordinarily means ‘learned ones’ or ‘poets’, but Parimelazhagan glosses it here as the devas, so that the heavenly world (புத்தேள் உலகு) ‘does not praise’ its own gods but the person whose fame fills the earth (நிலவரை, ‘to the bounds of the land’); Mu. Varadarasan follows this, and Pope renders it as heaven ceasing to laud the sage. Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read புலவர் as scholars or learned men. On any reading, Valluvar inverts the usual hierarchy in which heaven confers worth on earth: here the earth’s verdict, expressed as lasting renown, is what heaven itself acknowledges. A striking parallel is the Mahabharata story of King Indradyumna, who fell from heaven when his earthly reputation faded and regained it once living memory of his generosity was found.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The report of virtuous deeds spreadeth over the earth and ascendeth to heaven. As long as that report lasts, so long is the doer said to be in heaven.”
hinduism.explanation: King Indradyumna falls from heaven because no one remembers him; when an ancient tortoise recalls his lavish gifts, a celestial car returns him to heaven with these verses.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s claim: a person’s standing in heaven depends on the endurance of their renown on earth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 198 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: earthly fame from giving determines heavenly status.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat.”
christianity.explanation: In the judgment scene, the King welcomes into the kingdom those who fed the hungry and cared for strangers.
christianity.tie_back: Heaven honours people for what they did on earth for others, echoing the Kural’s heaven that honours the earthly giver.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared idea of heaven honouring earthly deeds of giving; no notion of fame or of heaven preferring humans over its own.

islam.quote_or_event: “All the inhabitants of the Heaven would love him, and then he is granted the pleasure of the people on the earth.”
islam.explanation: When God loves a servant, Gabriel announces it in heaven, all heaven’s inhabitants love that person, and then acceptance is placed for him among people on earth.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link heavenly esteem and earthly esteem for a person; the direction is reversed (heaven first in the hadith, earth first in the Kural).
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel link between celestial and earthly regard; the order of cause and effect is inverted.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name above the most sacred and powerful distinctions in Jewish life.
judaism.tie_back: Just as the Kural places earthly renown above even celestial sages, the Mishnah places a good name above priesthood and Torah learning.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:13 (trans. Joshua Kulp; numbered 4:17 in some editions)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on a good name outranking sacred status; no heavenly-realm imagery.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As kinsmen welcome a dear one on arrival, even so his own good deeds will welcome the doer of good who has gone from this world to the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a doer of good is greeted in the next world by his own good deeds, like a traveller welcomed home by relatives.
buddhism.tie_back: In both, what a person did on earth determines the welcome they receive in the higher world.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shared idea of earthly deeds honoured beyond this world; the welcomer is one’s karma, not the gods, and fame is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “After him I saw mighty Hercules, but it was his phantom only, for he is feasting ever with the immortal gods, and has lovely Hebe to wife.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus sees only Heracles’ shade in Hades, because the hero himself, after his earthly labours, was taken up to live among the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles’ renowned deeds on earth won him a seat of honour among the immortals, much as Valluvar’s earthly renown wins heaven’s praise.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel of earthly achievement earning divine honour; Heracles’ glory is heroic labour, not generosity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “What would not a man give if he might converse with Orpheus and Musaeus and Hesiod and Homer?”
philosophy.explanation: Facing death, Socrates imagines an afterlife where he could meet the renowned figures of the past, and counts that prospect a great good.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates pictures the next world as a place where the famous of the earth are sought out and honoured, loosely echoing the Kural’s heaven that honours the earthly renowned.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak but real parallel; Socrates is speculative and speaks of conversing, not of heaven ranking humans above gods.

kurals.tamil:
நத்தம்போல் கேடும் உளதாகும் சாக்காடும்
வித்தகர்க் கல்லால் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Naththampol kedum uladhaakum saakkaadum
Viththakarkku allaal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: A loss that is really an increase, and a death that is really a way of living on: these are hard for anyone to achieve except the truly wise.
kurals.elementary: A candle gets smaller as it burns, but it lights up the whole room. Some very wise people are like that. When they give away their time, money, or even their life for others, they seem to lose, but their goodness grows and people remember them forever.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s most paradoxical and textually difficult couplet. நத்தம் is glossed by Parimelazhagan as ஆக்கம் (increase), giving ‘a ruin that is like gain’: the loss suffered by the physical body (poverty through giving, hardship) that enlarges the ‘body of fame’ (புகழுடம்பு). சாக்காடும் உளதாகும், ‘death that becomes existence’, refers to dying in such a way that one’s renown is fixed for ever. Only the வித்தகர் (the skilled, the wise) manage this conversion of loss into gain. Commentators including Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah explain it through the Tamil idea of two bodies, the perishing body of flesh and the enduring body of renown. Cross-culturally it matches the logic of heroic or sacrificial death: Achilles’ choice at Troy, Diotima’s account of those who die ‘for the sake of leaving behind them a name’, and the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, either you will be killed on the battlefield and attain the heavenly planets, or you will conquer and enjoy the earthly kingdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that a righteous warrior cannot lose: death in duty brings heaven, and victory brings the kingdom.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a rightly met death not as loss but as a form of gain.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel on death transformed into gain; the Gita’s frame is dharma and heaven, with reputation addressed separately in 2.34.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a seed that must die in the soil in order to produce a harvest, pointing to his own death.
christianity.tie_back: The same paradox as the Kural: an apparent loss or death that is actually increase.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (death as fruitful gain); the fruit is spiritual, not renown.

islam.quote_or_event: “And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allāh as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an declares that those who die in God’s cause are not truly dead but living and provided for.
islam.tie_back: Both describe a death that is actually a continued life, ‘death that becomes existence’.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on death-as-life; the continued life is with God rather than in human memory.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth pairs the value of a good name with the claim that the day of death surpasses the day of birth, since only at death is a life’s name complete.
judaism.tie_back: Death that seals a good name is better than a beginning: close to the Kural’s death that establishes lasting renown.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on death completing a good name; Qoheleth’s tone is more sober and paradoxical than celebratory.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jataka the Bodhisatta, born as a hare with nothing else to give, leaps into a fire to offer his own body as food to a brahmin, who is Sakka in disguise. The fire turns icy and does not burn him, and Sakka marks the sign of a hare on the moon so that the hare’s virtue will be known throughout the aeon.
buddhism.explanation: The hare’s willingness to give up his life is converted into an everlasting sign in the sky.
buddhism.tie_back: A self-sacrifice that should have been pure loss becomes lasting renown, the very conversion the Kural credits to the wise.
buddhism.source: Jataka No. 316, Sasa-Jataka (ed. E.B. Cowell, Vol. III)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on sacrifice turned into eternal fame; the hare does not actually die in the Cowell version.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “If I stay here and fight, I shall not return alive but my name will live for ever: whereas if I go home my name will die, but it will be long ere death shall take me.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles explains his two possible fates: early death at Troy with undying fame, or a long, obscure life at home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The classic statement of trading the body’s life for a name that lives forever, the Kural’s ‘death that becomes existence’.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on death purchasing lasting renown; Achilles’ glory is martial, not generous.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They are ready to run all risks greater far than they would have for their children, and to spend money and undergo any sort of toil, and even to die, for the sake of leaving behind them a name which shall be eternal.”
philosophy.explanation: Diotima tells Socrates that the love of immortal fame drives people to spend, toil and even die, citing Alcestis, Achilles and Codrus.
philosophy.tie_back: Both identify the paradoxical exchange of wealth and even life for an undying name.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close; Plato treats fame-love as a lower rung on the ladder toward the Good, whereas Valluvar treats renown as a final good.

kurals.tamil:
தோன்றின் புகழொடு தோன்றுக அஃதிலார்
தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thondrin pukazhodu thondruka aqdhilaar
Thondralin thondraamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: If you appear before the world, appear with the qualities that bring renown; for those who lack them, it would be better not to appear at all.
kurals.elementary: If you’re going to step onto the stage in the school play, practise hard and do your best. Showing up and doing nothing good can be worse than not showing up at all. Whatever you take part in, do it in a way people can be proud of.
kurals.university: The verb தோன்று (‘to appear, arise, be born’) occurs five times, giving the couplet an incantatory force. Two readings exist. Parimelazhagan and Pope take it as ‘being born’: if one is born, one should be born with qualities that bring renown, and for those without them it were better not to be born (Pope: ‘’twere better hide your face’). Mu. Varadarasan and Karunanidhi read it as ‘appearing in a field’: whatever role or arena one enters, one should enter it with distinction, or not at all. The first reading is existential, the second vocational; both insist that visibility without merit is a net negative. The thought has sharp parallels: Jesus’ ‘good for that man if he had not been born’, Qoheleth’s preference for an untimely birth over a life empty of good, and the Mahabharata heroine Vidula’s maxim that it is ‘better to blaze up for a moment than smoke for ever’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is better to blaze up for a moment than smoke for ever and ever.”
hinduism.explanation: Queen Vidula rebukes her son Sanjaya, who lies despondent after defeat, urging him to win distinction by his deeds rather than live on without honour.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it prefers a brief appearance with glory to a long existence without it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 133 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Vidula’s context is martial honour, while the Kural is broader.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It had been good for that man if he had not been born.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says this of the one who would betray him, Judas.
christianity.tie_back: The same judgement form as the Kural: some lives would have been better never begun.
christianity._accuracy_note: Identical structure; the cause is a grave betrayal rather than a mere lack of renown.

islam.quote_or_event: “The disbeliever will say, “Oh, I wish that I were dust!””
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, seeing what his own hands have sent forth, the disbeliever wishes he had never existed as a person at all.
islam.tie_back: A life lived without worth leads to the wish for non-existence, echoing the Kural’s ‘better not to appear’.
islam._accuracy_note: Next-best parallel; eschatological regret rather than an ethical maxim about renown.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth says that a long, prolific life that never attains good, and ends without honourable burial, is worse than never having been born.
judaism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: existence without the good (and without honour at the end) is worse than non-appearance.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong structural and thematic match; ‘good’ here means satisfaction as much as moral worth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists the qualities by which a person’s glory steadily increases.
buddhism.tie_back: It names the qualities with which one should ‘appear’: those that naturally produce renown.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Supports the positive half (appear with renown-bearing qualities); lacks the ‘better not to appear’ half.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It becomes us, therefore, to take our stand at the head of all the Lycians and bear the brunt of the fight.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Sarpedon tells Glaucus that because they enjoy honour and privilege as princes, they must justify it by fighting in the front ranks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Those who appear in a prominent place must appear with deeds worthy of renown, or their position is empty.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the vocational reading (appearing in a role with distinction); martial context.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Honour is the prize of virtue, and it is to the good that it is rendered.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, discussing the great-souled person, says honour is properly given only to the genuinely good.
philosophy.tie_back: Renown should accompany real excellence; one who seeks the stage without virtue has no claim to it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on renown tied to virtue; Aristotle does not say the unworthy would be better unborn.

kurals.tamil:
புகழ்பட வாழாதார் தந்நோவார் தம்மை
இகழ்வாரை நோவது எவன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pukazhpada vaazhaadhaar thannovaar thammai
Ikazhvaarai novadhu evan?
kurals.meaning: Those who fail to live in a way that earns renown should grieve over themselves; why do they instead resent the people who look down on them?
kurals.elementary: If you didn’t study and got a bad grade, being angry at the teacher doesn’t help. It’s better to look at what you could do differently. The same goes for what people think of you: if they don’t think well of you, first check your own actions.
kurals.university: Valluvar turns from praising renown to diagnosing a common evasion: blaming one’s critics instead of oneself. The couplet sets தந்நோவார் (‘they do not grieve over themselves’) against இகழ்வாரை நோவது (‘resenting those who scorn them’) and ends in the rhetorical எவன், ‘why?’. The ethical claim is that reputation, though it lives in others’ mouths (Kural 232), is earned by one’s own conduct, so responsibility lies within. Commentators from Parimelazhagan to Karunanidhi read it as a call to self-correction rather than to resentment. The insight is widely shared: Jesus’ mote and beam, Lamentations’ question why a living man should complain of the punishment of his own sins, Zeus’s complaint in the Odyssey that mortals blame the gods for their own folly, and Epictetus’ portrait of the uninstructed person who lays the fault of his condition on others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man must elevate himself by his own mind, not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that each person is responsible for lifting or lowering themselves; the self is its own friend or enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: Both locate the cause of one’s standing within oneself, not in others.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on self-responsibility; the Gita addresses spiritual elevation rather than public reputation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes those who fixate on others’ small faults while ignoring their own large ones.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s renownless person resents critics instead of examining himself: the same misplaced focus.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on self-examination before blaming others; not specifically about reputation.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whatever strikes you of disaster - it is for what your hands have earned; but He pardons much.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that misfortunes people suffer are largely the result of their own deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Kural traces a poor reputation to one’s own conduct; the Qur’an traces misfortune to one’s own hands.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on self-caused outcomes; broader than reputation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations asks why anyone should complain about suffering that follows from their own wrongdoing, and urges self-examination instead.
judaism.tie_back: Nearly the same rhetorical question as the Kural’s எவன் (‘why?’): why resent consequences you brought on yourself?
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in form and logic; concerns punishment rather than scorn.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells people to stop scrutinising others’ failures and to look at their own deeds, both done and left undone.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s advice exactly: look at what you failed to do, not at those who criticise you.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; ‘undone’ acts match the Kural’s failure to live renownedly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “See now, how men lay blame upon us gods for what is after all nothing but their own folly.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Opening the Odyssey, Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for troubles they bring on themselves, citing Aegisthus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same diagnosis as the Kural: people blame outside forces for what their own conduct produced.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close on misplaced blame; the targets are gods rather than human critics.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “An uninstructed person will lay the fault of his own bad condition upon others. Someone just starting instruction will lay the fault on himself.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus describes stages of moral progress: blaming others, then blaming oneself, and finally blaming no one.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar asks the renownless to take Epictetus’ second step: turn the blame inward rather than on critics.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on self-attribution; Epictetus would also deny that reputation matters at all.

kurals.tamil:
வசையென்ப வையத்தார்க் கெல்லாம் இசையென்னும்
எச்சம் பெறாஅ விடின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vasaiyenba vaiyaththaarkku ellaam isaiyennum
Echcham peraaa vidin.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that for anyone on earth it is a disgrace to fail to leave behind the legacy called renown.
kurals.elementary: A good camper leaves the campsite better than they found it, maybe with a helpful sign for the next visitors. Life is similar: it’s a shame to leave without leaving behind something good that people remember you by.
kurals.university: The pivotal word is எச்சம்: ‘remainder, residue, what is left over’, and by extension ‘offspring’ or ‘legacy’. Renown (இசை) is defined as the proper residue of a life; to fail to obtain it (பெறாஅ, with the poetic vowel-lengthening called அளபெடை) is வசை, reproach, and the plural subject வையத்தார்க் கெல்லாம் makes the standard universal. Pope captured the offspring sense: ‘Fame is virtue’s child, they say; if, then, / You childless live, you live the scorn of men.’ The idea that a person’s true progeny is their good name has a remarkable parallel in Isaiah 56:5, where the childless are promised ‘a name better than of sons and of daughters’, and in Diotima’s speech in Plato’s Symposium, where the ‘children’ of Homer and Lycurgus are their works. The Islamic teaching on what continues after death (ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, a righteous child) offers a devotional analogue: what a person leaves behind continues to count.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Your enemies will describe you in many unkind words and scorn your ability. What could be more painful for you?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that abandoning his duty would leave him an object of public scorn, the most painful outcome of all.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat the world’s reproach, for failing to achieve what earns honour, as a real and bitter disgrace.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on public reproach for failing to earn honour; lacks the legacy/offspring dimension of எச்சம்.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews says that Abel’s righteous offering still ‘speaks’ long after his death.
christianity.tie_back: A good deed as the part of a person that remains and keeps speaking: the Kural’s எச்சம் of renown.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on legacy that outlives death; no idea of disgrace for failing to leave one.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet names three things that keep benefiting a person after death: ongoing charity (sadaqah jariyah), useful knowledge, and a righteous child.
islam.tie_back: An exact counterpart to எச்சம், the ‘remainder’ a life leaves behind, even including the offspring sense of the word.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on legacy that outlives death; the benefit is reward for the deceased rather than reputation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.”
judaism.explanation: God promises faithful eunuchs, who can have no children, an everlasting name that is better than descendants.
judaism.tie_back: Precisely Pope’s reading of the Kural: renown is the offspring that outlasts a life, better than sons and daughters.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on name-as-offspring; the name is granted by God for faithfulness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As from a great heap of flowers many garlands can be made, even so should many good deeds be done by one born a mortal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada urges every mortal to make the most of the material of life by producing many good deeds.
buddhism.tie_back: Both treat a human life as something that ought to leave a worthy product behind.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel on the obligation to produce good from a mortal life; no reference to reputation or disgrace.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Let me not then die ingloriously and without a struggle, but let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Realising he is doomed before Achilles, Hector resolves to leave behind at least a deed that will be told in the future.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hector’s last wish is the Kural’s எச்சம்: not to leave the world without a remainder of renown.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on refusing to die without a lasting name.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Who, when he thinks of Homer and Hesiod and other great poets, would not rather have their children than ordinary human ones?”
philosophy.explanation: Diotima argues that great works and laws are ‘children of the soul’ that bring their parents everlasting glory, more precious than physical offspring.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ‘offspring called renown’: a legacy of fame as a truer child than any bodily heir.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on fame as offspring; Plato places this below the vision of Beauty itself.

kurals.tamil:
வசையிலா வண்பயன் குன்றும் இசையிலா
யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vasaiyilaa vanpayan kundrum isaiyilaa
Yaakkai poruththa nilam.
kurals.meaning: The land that carries the body of a person without renown will see its rich, faultless harvest decline.
kurals.elementary: Think of a garden where one plant takes all the water and sunshine but never gives flowers or fruit. The whole garden does a little worse because of it. A person who takes from the world but gives nothing good back is a bit like that plant.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar moves from social reproach to cosmic consequence: the earth (நிலம்) that ‘bears’ (பொறுத்த) a renownless body (இசையிலா யாக்கை) suffers a decline (குன்றும்) in its bountiful, faultless yield (வசையிலா வண்பயன்). The choice of யாக்கை, the bare physical frame, pointedly denies such a person any fuller identity: they are mere body, a burden on the ground. The underlying belief, common to many ancient cultures, links moral quality to fertility: righteous people and rulers bring rain and harvest, the unrighteous bring dearth, an idea found in the Gita’s cycle of rain and sacrifice, the Buddha’s discourse on unprincipled kings, and Homer’s blameless king under whom the earth yields abundantly. Modern readers may take it as a vivid image of free-riding: a life that consumes without contributing diminishes the common stock, close to Cicero’s charge that the self-absorbed are ‘traitors to social life’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “All living bodies subsist on food grains, which are produced from rain. Rains are produced by performance of yajña [sacrifice], and yajña is born of prescribed duties.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a cycle in which rightful action sustains the rain that feeds the crops that feed all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: In both, the fertility of the land depends on how human beings conduct themselves.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the moral-fertility link; framed through sacrificial duty, not renown.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, an owner finds a fig tree barren for three years and asks why it should keep taking up the soil.
christianity.tie_back: The fruitless tree ‘cumbers the ground’ just as the renownless body burdens the land in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close image of a fruitless life burdening the soil; the Kural adds that the land’s own yield declines.

islam.quote_or_event: “Corruption has appeared throughout the land and sea by [reason of] what the hands of people have earned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an attributes disorder and ruin on land and sea to human wrongdoing.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see the earth’s well-being as damaged by the moral failures of those who live on it.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on moral failure harming the land; concerns active corruption rather than a life lacking renown.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.”
judaism.explanation: After Cain murders Abel, God tells him the ground will no longer give him its strength.
judaism.tie_back: The land’s yield diminishes because of the moral state of the one who lives on it, as in the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear moral-fertility link; Cain’s crime is murder, far graver than a lack of renown.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When the people of town and country are unprincipled, the courses of the moon and sun become erratic.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a chain in which unprincipled rulers and people lead to erratic seasons, insufficient rain, badly ripening crops and sickly people, and the reverse when people are principled.
buddhism.tie_back: Human moral quality directly affects the land’s produce, exactly as the Kural claims.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on morality affecting harvests; concerns unprincipled conduct generally rather than lack of renown.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees are loaded with fruit, the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The disguised Odysseus tells Penelope that her fame reaches heaven like that of a blameless king whose virtue makes land and sea abundant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The positive mirror image of the Kural: virtue and renown make the land fruitful, so their absence would make it fail.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close in reverse (renowned virtue produces abundance); refers to a king rather than any person.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They are traitors to social life, for they contribute to it none of their interest, none of their effort, none of their means.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero condemns those who, absorbed in their own affairs, give nothing to the common life of society.
philosophy.tie_back: The rationalist version of the Kural: a life that takes but contributes nothing diminishes the shared stock.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.29 (trans. Walter Miller)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on the non-contributing life as a harm to all; no agricultural or cosmic dimension.

kurals.tamil:
வசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் இசையொழிய
வாழ்வாரே வாழா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vasaiyozhiya vaazhvaare vaazhvaar isaiyozhiya
Vaazhvaare vaazhaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who live free of reproach are the ones who truly live; those who live without renown, though alive, do not really live.
kurals.elementary: Being alive is like being given a notebook. Some people fill it with kind, brave, helpful stories. Others leave it empty or scribble unkind things. Valluvar says only the first kind are really ‘living’; the others just have the notebook.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a chiastic couplet built on repetition: வசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் / இசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழாதவர். The halves pivot on a near-rhyme, வசை (blame) and இசை (renown), so that ‘living without blame’ and ‘living without renown’ sound almost identical yet lead to opposite verdicts. The emphatic particle ஏ marks exclusivity: only the blameless truly live; the renownless are precisely the not-living. Life is thus redefined qualitatively rather than biologically. Similar ideas appear in the Talmudic teaching that the wicked are called dead even in their lifetimes, the Dhammapada’s ‘the heedless are as if dead already’, the Gita’s verdict that the self-indulgent person ‘lives in vain’, and Revelation’s church that has ‘a name that thou livest, and art dead’. Valluvar’s distinctive move is to make renown, the social trace of virtue, the test of whether one has lived at all.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man who does not follow this prescribed Vedic system of sacrifice certainly leads a life of sin, for a person delighting only in the senses lives in vain.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the self-indulgent person who ignores the cycle of duty and sacrifice ‘lives in vain’ (moghaṁ jīvati).
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts deny that mere biological life counts as living; a life empty of worth is in vain.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on ‘living in vain’; the Gita’s criterion is duty and sacrifice rather than renown.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church in Sardis that despite its reputation for being alive, it is spiritually dead.
christianity.tie_back: Both separate true life from mere appearance of life; Revelation warns that a name must reflect real works.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on ‘alive yet dead’; ironically, here the reputation for life is false, reminding that renown must rest on real virtue.

islam.quote_or_event: “And is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him light by which to walk among the people like one who is in darkness, never to emerge therefrom?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the guided person as someone brought from death to life, contrasted with one who stays in darkness.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats true life as a moral and spiritual state rather than mere breath.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on qualitative life versus death; the criterion is faith and guidance, not renown.

judaism.quote_or_event: “These are the wicked, who even during their lives are called dead.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud contrasts the righteous, called living even after death, with the wicked, who are called dead while still alive.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact verdict: the blameless truly live, and those without worth are the ‘not-living’ even while alive.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; the Talmud’s criterion is righteousness rather than renown as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that careless, unmindful people are effectively dead even while living, while the heedful do not die.
buddhism.tie_back: The same redefinition of life and death by quality of living that the Kural makes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on ‘alive yet dead’; the criterion is heedfulness, not reputation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld, Achilles, the very emblem of undying glory, tells Odysseus that even the humblest life on earth is better than all his fame among the dead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A deliberate counterpoint: Homer lets his greatest hero question whether renown can compensate for life itself, the opposite of the Kural’s verdict.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Honest contrast rather than parallel; shows the tension within Greek heroic culture over the worth of fame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The life which is unexamined is not worth living.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial, Socrates says a life without moral self-examination is not worth living.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Socrates sets a qualitative test for whether a life counts; the test is self-examination rather than renown.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that some lives do not count as true living; Socrates explicitly disregards public opinion, unlike the Kural.
